title: Parachute Wells: Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Parachute wells have a 120-foot median depth, with typical completed-well costs of $12,000-$21,000.
h1: What Parachute Well Records Show Buyers
intro_html:
For rural property around Parachute, the local well records point to moderate drilling depths and generally strong reported yields. Among 695 permitted wells within 5 miles, the median reported depth is 120 feet, and the median reported pump yield is 15.0 gallons per minute.

Those figures are useful for planning, but they are not a guarantee for a specific parcel. Only 439 records report total depth, 105 report pump yield, and 35 report a static water level. A buyer should treat the nearby permit map, well construction report, and a driller’s site-specific opinion as separate pieces of the decision.

sections.heading: Parachute well depth depends on the local formation
sections.html:
Parachute wells have a median depth of 120 feet. The middle half runs from 50 to 174 feet, while the 90th-percentile depth is 213 feet. The deepest recorded well is 390 feet.

Depths are split fairly evenly between shallow and moderate drilling: 46% are under 100 feet, and 52% fall from 100 to 300 feet. Only 2% are from 300 to 600 feet, with none recorded at 600 feet or deeper. Most permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, while 7 are alluvial and 27 name the Wasatch-Fort Union. That mix matters because fractured rock can change sharply over short distances. Ask for a bid with a realistic depth range, not a promise based only on the median.

sections.heading: Reported well yields near Parachute are usually workable
sections.html:
The median reported yield is 15.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 10.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. In the available yield records, 51% produce more than 15 gallons per minute and 43% produce from 5 to 15 gallons per minute.

Low-producing wells are present but uncommon in this dataset: 5% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute and 1% report under 1 gallon per minute. Yield is not the same as storage in the well or guaranteed household supply. A pump test, recovery information, storage tank sizing, and the permitted use all deserve review. Domestic and household wells make up 51% of the use mix, while monitoring wells account for 29%, so not every nearby record is a direct comparison to a home well.

sections.heading: Water levels in Parachute records need a closer look
sections.html:
The median static water level is 57 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 29 to 90 feet. That gives a useful first estimate for pump setting and trench planning, but the number varies by location, season, construction, and measurement date.

The decade figures show a deeper reported median in the 2020s than in the 2000s: 57 feet below surface compared with 22 feet. That pattern suggests water was measured farther below ground in the newer decade, but it does not prove a basin-wide decline. The records are limited to 35 reported static water levels and may not compare the same wells. Before buying, check the original well construction reports and ask whether a current water-level measurement is available for the specific property.

sections.heading: Permit history shows long use and current drilling activity
sections.html:
Garfield County records show permitted wells around Parachute from the 1950s through the 2020s, with the newest permit year listed as 2026. The busiest decades were the 1990s, with 179 permits, and the 2000s, with 172. There were 94 in the 2010s and 38 in the 2020s.

Shelton Drilling Corporation, listed with Shelton, Wayne, appears most often in the records, with 214 wells. Authorized, listed with Pe, Pg, appears on 67, and Collins Drilling Co, listed with Collins, F. E. “Bodie,” appears on 23. These names help identify local history, but an older permit does not establish present well performance. Confirm the driller, permit conditions, completion report, and any later pump or water-quality work before relying on the record.

sections.heading: A Parachute well commonly costs $12,000 to $21,000 finished
sections.html:
The local drilling model uses a typical rate of $50 to $75 per foot for mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. At the 120-foot median depth, drilling the hole alone is estimated at about $6,000 to $9,000.

A finished system, including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, is estimated at $12,000 to $21,000. The final price can move outside that range if the hole is deeper, access is difficult, casing or grout requirements change, or the lot needs longer utility runs. Get the bid in writing with depth assumptions, casing and grout, pump equipment, testing, electrical, trenching, and unsuccessful-hole terms spelled out. A low drilling quote is not comparable if it leaves out the completion work.

sections.heading: Parachute buyers should check water quality, yield, and site limits
sections.html:
Mapped environmental information deserves attention before closing. Within about 10 miles, the records show 826 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 14 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. These mapped sites do not by themselves prove that a particular well is contaminated, but they are a reason to order a current laboratory water test and review nearby land uses.

Also investigate low yield, dry-hole risk, and septic separation. A well permit controls allowed use; an exempt household-use well can have specific limits, including the 35-gallon-per-minute exempt-well pumping limit. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be needed. Confirm the well permit, septic approval, legal access, building envelope, and utility route before assuming the lot can support a home.

sections.heading: Use neighboring wells before committing to a Parachute lot
sections.html:
Start with the closest comparable permits, especially domestic wells in Battlement Mesa and the surrounding Parachute area. Compare reported depth, aquifer description, yield, static water level, construction, and permit use rather than looking at one attractive result. The nearby records show that most wells are in the unnamed or fractured-bedrock category, where results can vary between adjacent sites.

For a purchase, make the well permit and construction report part of due diligence. Ask for a flow test, water-quality test, pump details, and a contractor’s estimate based on the actual access route. For a new build, confirm septic setbacks, driveway access, electrical service, trenching, and the legal water supply before finalizing plans. Rifle, Silt, and Battlement Mesa can provide broader regional comparisons, but the parcel’s nearest wells remain the more useful starting point.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Parachute, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Parachute is 120 feet. The middle half runs from 50 to 174 feet, and the 90th-percentile depth is 213 feet. About 46% are under 100 feet, while 52% are from 100 to 300 feet. A specific lot can differ, especially in fractured bedrock.

faq.q: What does a well cost to drill in Parachute?
faq.a: The local model uses $50 to $75 per foot. At the 120-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $6,000 to $9,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $12,000 to $21,000. Confirm what each contractor includes before comparing bids.

faq.q: How much water do Parachute wells produce?
faq.a: The median reported yield is 15.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 10.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. More than 15 gallons per minute is reported by 51% of wells with yield data. Only 1% report under 1 gallon per minute, but a pump test is still important for the individual property.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Parachute?
faq.a: The permit map cannot establish whether a particular well is safe to drink. About 10 miles around Parachute, records show 826 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 14 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Order a current laboratory test for the property’s well and review the results before relying on it.

faq.q: Are water levels dropping near Parachute?
faq.a: Reported static water levels have a median of 22 feet below surface in the 2000s and 57 feet in the 2020s. That suggests newer measurements were deeper, but only 35 records report static water level and the wells may not be comparable. The figures do not prove a basin-wide decline; check the specific well’s history.
